abstract:
During non-rapid eye movement (NREM) sleep, cortical neurons alternate between ON periods of firing and OFF periods of silence, the latter accounting for the slow waves of the EEG. Converging evidence indicates that OFF periods can also occur locally during extended wake ("local sleep"), at a behavioral cost, but whether this phenomenon is ubiquitous across the cortex, whether some areas are more resilient than others, and whether it can also provide any benefit, remain open questions. Here we recorded from 11 cortical areas (and claustrum) in 15 rats using high-density Neuropixels probes and detected OFF periods with a novel method that captures spatially restricted and irregularly shaped events mischaracterized or missed by traditional methods. We found OFF periods during extended wake in every region tested, with no evidence that any area is spared. Over the course of sleep deprivation, OFF periods became more frequent, longer, larger, and quieter, and their features correlated with delta power on a per-event basis in both wake and NREM sleep, consistent with the notion that they reflect accumulating sleep need. The extent to which OFF periods overlapped across areas also increased across sleep deprivation. Finally, the rate of medium and large OFF periods during sleep deprivation was negatively correlated with their rebound in subsequent recovery sleep, consistent with the possibility that local sleep in wake partially discharges sleep need before the animal falls asleep.

Statement of SignificanceProlonged wakefulness drives small groups of cortical neurons into brief sleep-like states even as the animal remains awake and behaving. This "local sleep" in wake is thought to underlie the errors and slowed responses of sleep deprivation, but how widespread it is, and whether it helps, remains unclear. Using high-density recordings across many cortical regions in the rat and a novel detection method sensitive to small, irregular events, we show that local sleep is not confined to a few vulnerable areas but occurs throughout the cortex, growing with accumulating sleep need. We also find that these neuronal lapses may begin to relieve that need before sleep takes over, suggesting that they may represent an early, piecemeal form of recovery.
